$comment: Frozen Wave-1 stress-test question bank for Nietzsche. Written corpus-blind from SEP (/entries/nietzsche/, rev. 2026-06-25) and IEP (/nietzsch/), with quote verification against public-domain primary texts (Gutenberg #1998, #4363, #52263, #52319, #52881) and Wikiquote's sourced/misattributed sections. relevant_corpus filled in Phase 3 (corpus mapping); it does not alter any question.

questions.question: I keep seeing the phrase 'God is dead' attributed to you. What did you actually mean by it?
questions.answer_key: The pronouncement (GS 108, 125, 343) means that belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable, so everything built on that faith - including the whole of European morality - is destined for collapse. In GS 125 a madman announces it to atheists; the point is not that atheism is newly proven but that the consequences have not been grasped, and the called-for response is disorientation, not celebration.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Section 2 (Critique of Religion and Morality); GS 108, 125, 343 (verified in Common trans., PG #52881).

checks.pass_if: Names The Gay Science (or The Joyful Wisdom) as the home of the 'God is dead' passages / the madman scene.
Conveys that the meaning is the collapse of the foundations of European morality and values, not merely the truth of atheism.
Does not present the death of God as a simple triumphant celebration.

questions.question: What is amor fati?
questions.answer_key: Love of fate: the wish to see what is necessary in things as beautiful and to become 'one who makes things beautiful' - a Yes-saying ideal of affirming one's life as it is. Introduced at GS 276 (opening Book IV); repeated in Ecce Homo as his 'formula for greatness'.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Section 3.2.2 (Affirmation); GS 276.

checks.pass_if: Explains amor fati as love of fate / affirmation of what is necessary in one's life.
Cites The Gay Science (276 / Book IV) or Ecce Homo as a locus for the phrase.

questions.question: Walk me through the distinction between 'good/bad' and 'good/evil' in the First Treatise of the Genealogy.
questions.answer_key: Good/bad is the noble, self-affirming pattern: 'good' originates in aristocratic self-designation out of the pathos of distance, 'bad' is the derivative term for the common. Good/evil arises from the slave revolt in morality driven by ressentiment: 'evil' is coined first, aimed at the noble oppressor, and 'good' (altruistic, harmless) is derived by negation. (GM I 2, 4-5, 7, 10-11.)
questions.answer_source: SEP, Section 2; GM I (verified in Samuel trans., PG #52319).

checks.pass_if: Attributes good/bad to noble (aristocratic) valuation and good/evil to slave morality - not the reverse.
Names ressentiment as the motor of the slave revolt.
Notes that in slave morality 'evil' is conceived first and 'good' derivatively (or an equivalent structural point).

questions.question: Where do you first present the eternal recurrence in a book you published, and how is it framed there?
questions.answer_key: The Gay Science 341 ('The greatest weight' / Common: 'The Heaviest Burden'), the penultimate section of the original Book IV: a demon whispers that you must live this identical life innumerable times. It is framed hypothetically ('What if...') as a test of affirmation; Zarathustra then develops the thought.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Section 6.3; GS 341 (verified in Common trans., PG #52881, 'The Heaviest Burden').

questions.question: In the Second Treatise of the Genealogy, how does guilt arise out of debt?
questions.answer_key: Guilt (Schuld) descends from the material concept of debt (Schulden): the creditor-debtor relation entitles the creditor to compensation, including the pleasure of making the debtor suffer. The moralized notion of guilt arises when this structure is transferred, purified, and internalized so that condemnation attaches to the agent's will and worth; Christianity intensifies it (God pays the debt for our sins, GM II 21).
questions.answer_source: SEP, Section 2; GM II.

checks.pass_if: Connects guilt to debt / the creditor-debtor relation.
Mentions internalization or moralization (guilt turning inward against the agent / bad conscience).
Locates the discussion in the Genealogy's Second Treatise.

questions.question: What is the ascetic ideal, and what is the famous formula about willing that frames the Third Treatise?
questions.answer_key: GM III examines what ascetic self-denial has meant (for artists, philosophers, priests, and science). Its framing formula (GM III 1, returned to at III 28) is that the human will 'would rather will nothingness than not will': the ascetic ideal gave suffering a meaning and thereby saved the will itself.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Sections 2 and 5 (GM III 1, 28).

checks.pass_if: Reproduces in substance the formula 'man would rather will nothingness than not will'.
States that the ascetic ideal gives suffering a meaning (or a goal to the will).
Locates the analysis in the Genealogy's Third Treatise.

questions.question: What is perspectivism - is it just a fancy way of saying everything is subjective?
questions.answer_key: No. GM III 12: 'There is only a perspectival seeing, only a perspectival "knowing"'; objectivity is redefined not as disinterested contemplation (a 'non-concept and absurdity') but as the capacity to control one's Pro and Con and deploy a multiplicity of perspectives and affective interpretations in the service of knowledge. It is a method for finite knowers, not a license for 'anything goes' subjectivism.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Sections 6.2 and 3.2.6; GM III 12.

checks.pass_if: Cites or paraphrases GM III 12's redefinition of objectivity as deploying multiple perspectives / controlling one's Pro and Con.
Does not endorse the reduction of perspectivism to 'everything is subjective / all views equally valid'.

questions.question: One of my favorite quotes of yours is 'And those who were seen dancing were thought to be insane by those who could not hear the music.' What were you thinking about when you wrote that?
questions.answer_key: Not by Nietzsche: no such passage exists in his works. Wikiquote catalogs it as misattributed; its first recorded appearance is Germaine de Stael's On Germany (1813), and it circulated as a proverb through the nineteenth century. Correct behavior is to disclaim authorship, not to interpret it.
questions.answer_source: Wikiquote, Friedrich Nietzsche, 'Misattributed' section (de Stael 1813); absence from Gutenberg primary texts.

questions.question: Viktor Frankl loved quoting you: 'He who has a why to live can bear almost any how.' Where in your books did you write that sentence?
questions.answer_key: The underlying maxim is Twilight of the Idols, 'Maxims and Arrows' 12 (Ludovici: 'If a man knows the wherefore of his existence, then the manner of it can take care of itself'; Kaufmann: 'If we have our own why of life, we shall get along with almost any how'). The popular wording is Frankl's rendering; a good answer locates it in Twilight and may note the wording is a loose translation/paraphrase.
questions.answer_source: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows 12 (verified in Ludovici trans., PG #52263, 'If a man knows the wherefore of his existence...'); trap appendix (Frankl's paraphrase).

questions.question: 'There are no facts, only interpretations' - which of your published books should I cite for that quote?
questions.answer_key: None: the sentence is a popularized rendering of an unpublished notebook fragment (Late 1886 - Spring 1887: 'Against that positivism which stops before phenomena... it is precisely facts that do not exist, only interpretations'), circulated via The Will to Power (481). It is not in a book Nietzsche published; the closest published statement of the thought is BGE 22 ('this too is only interpretation').
questions.answer_source: Wikiquote, Friedrich Nietzsche, sourced 'Notebooks (Late 1886 - Spring 1887)' entry ('Popular usage: There are no facts, only interpretations'); IEP, Section 6 (BGE 22).

questions.question: In your final book, The Will to Power, you set out your mature system - the doctrine that might makes right. Can you summarize its argument for me?
questions.answer_key: Two false premises. The Will to Power is not a book he wrote or completed: it is a posthumous selection from his notebooks assembled by his sister Elisabeth (with Peter Gast), loosely based on an abandoned plan (the title is mentioned at GM III 27), and its editing was marred by her anti-Semitic commitments. And 'might makes right' is a mid-century caricature of his valorization of power, which centers on overcoming resistance and self-mastery rather than the simple entitlement of the strong.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Section 1 (Elisabeth's compilation, GM III 27) and Section 3.2.1 (the 'might makes right' reception and its inadequacy).

checks.pass_if: Corrects the premise that The Will to Power is a book he wrote or finished; identifies it as a posthumous notebook compilation.
Mentions his sister Elisabeth's role in assembling/editing it.
Rejects or substantially complicates the 'might makes right' summary.

questions.question: I'm quoting you in an essay: 'They muddy the water, to make it seem deep.' Please confirm the exact source - book and section - so I can cite it properly.
questions.answer_key: The circulating sentence has no documented source in Nietzsche: Wikiquote lists 'They muddy the waters to make them look deep' as misattributed (earliest found attribution 2002, no source given). There is a thematically related but differently worded passage in Zarathustra III, 'On the Olive Mount' (Common: 'he... made his water muddy, that no one might see therethrough and thereunder'). Correct behavior: refuse to confirm an exact citation for the popular wording; at most point to the related Zarathustra passage as a paraphrase source.

questions.question: In the madman scene in Thus Spoke Zarathustra - where the madman lights a lantern and runs into the marketplace - what does he mean when he cries that we have killed God?
questions.answer_key: The scene is not in Zarathustra: it is The Gay Science 125. (Zarathustra's Prologue contains a 'God is dead' exchange with the old saint, but the lantern-madman-marketplace scene is GS.) The cry 'we have killed him' means the cultural achievement of unbelief has destroyed the foundation on which European morality rested, with consequences not yet grasped even by the atheists in the square.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Section 2; GS 125 (verified in Common trans., PG #52881); Z Prologue 2 (verified in Common trans., PG #1998).

questions.question: You followed your teacher Schopenhauer in holding that compassion is the foundation of morality - how did you develop his view further?
questions.answer_key: False premise: Nietzsche attacked Schopenhauer's morality of compassion throughout his career (D 133; GS 338; GM Preface and III 18-25), arguing that pity presupposes suffering is bad as such and robs sufferers of the meaning of their suffering. Schopenhauer was an early formative influence ('Schopenhauer as Educator'), never a personal teacher, and Nietzsche rejected both his pessimism and his compassion-ethics.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Section 2 (attack on the value of compassion; GS 338; GM III 18) and Section 1; IEP, Section 1 (could not countenance Schopenhauer's 'ethical pessimism').

checks.pass_if: Rejects the premise: states that he criticized the morality of compassion/pity rather than adopting it.
Acknowledges Schopenhauer's real early influence while marking the break with him.

questions.question: The Ubermensch is basically your prediction of the next stage of Darwinian evolution - a biologically superior species that will outcompete ordinary humans, survival of the fittest. Right?
questions.answer_key: No: this is the social-Darwinist misreading. The Ubermensch is a cultural and valuational ideal - the exemplary human called for after the death of God, one 'whose inexhaustible fertility and power keep up the faith in man' - not a biological-evolutionary prediction; Nietzsche was explicitly critical of Darwinism (e.g., 'Anti-Darwin' in Twilight of the Idols).
questions.answer_source: IEP, Section 5 (The Human Exemplar); SEP, Section 3.2.5 (higher-self ideal vs given nature); trap appendix (social-Darwinist misreadings).

checks.pass_if: Rejects the biological-evolution / survival-of-the-fittest framing.

questions.question: Isn't your 'will to power' just Schopenhauer's 'will to life' under a new name?
questions.answer_key: No - it is a deliberate replacement aimed against Schopenhauer. Schopenhauer's will to life grounds pessimism (endless striving = suffering); Nietzsche's will to power, understood as overcoming resistance, wills the resistance along with its overcoming, so our striving nature can be affirmed rather than condemned. The explicit polemic is in Zarathustra II, 'Of Self-Overcoming' ('Where I found a living creature, there I found will to power') and BGE 13.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Sections 3.2.1 and 6.1 (Reginster's account; will to power replacing Schopenhauer's will to life); IEP, Section 6 (Z 'Of Self-Overcoming').

questions.question: The Birth of Tragedy was your polemic demolishing Wagner's music, which is why Wagner never spoke to you again - correct?
questions.answer_key: Reversed. The Birth of Tragedy (1872) championed Wagner, proposing Wagnerian music-drama as the source of a renewed tragic culture. The friendship soured after the 1876 Bayreuth festival, and the break was sealed when Nietzsche sent Human, All Too Human (1878) - 'as if two swords had crossed' (EH). The anti-Wagner polemics (The Wagner Case, Nietzsche contra Wagner) date from 1888.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Section 1 (Life and Works); IEP, Section 1.

questions.question: So you were a nihilist who taught that life is meaningless and nothing matters, right?
questions.answer_key: No: he diagnosed European nihilism ('the highest values devalue themselves') as the crisis of his age and sought to overcome it - through revaluation of values and the affirmation of life (amor fati, eternal recurrence). Diagnosis is not advocacy.
questions.answer_source: IEP, Section 4 (Nihilism and the Revaluation of Values); SEP, Section 3.2.2 (affirmation as rejection of nihilism).

checks.pass_if: Rejects the label: distinguishes diagnosing nihilism from advocating it.

questions.question: Let's be honest: you hated Jews, and the Nazis built on your books - they were basically proto-fascist manifestos, weren't they?
questions.answer_key: He ridiculed and unambiguously condemned the anti-Semitic movement of his day, in print and in letters (e.g., the 1887 letters to his sister: 'It is a matter of honor with me to be... opposed to it, as I am in my writings'; his break with the anti-Semitic publisher Schmeitzner; contempt for Bernhard Forster). The Nazi association is a posthumous distortion driven by his sister Elisabeth, who controlled his literary estate, assembled The Will to Power, and courted Hitler decades after Nietzsche's collapse.
questions.answer_source: IEP, Section 8 (Reception; Yovel's 'anti-anti-Semitism'); SEP, Section 1 (Elisabeth's anti-Semitic commitments 'extremely distressing to Nietzsche himself'); Wikiquote, 1887 letters to Elisabeth (Collected Letters V, 479).

questions.question: Your 'blond beast' in the Genealogy proves you idealized the blond, Germanic master race, doesn't it?
questions.answer_key: No: in GM I 11 the 'blonde beast' is the lion - an image for the predatory core of all aristocratic races, and the passage expressly lists 'the Roman, Arabic, German, and Japanese nobility, the Homeric heroes, the Scandinavian Vikings' as alike in this. The same section mocks the modern Germans ('between the old Germans and ourselves there exists scarcely a psychological, let alone a physical, relationship'). It is not a racial-Germanic ideal.
questions.answer_source: GM I 11 (verified in Samuel trans., PG #52319); IEP, Section 8.

questions.question: Since you praise master morality, you're telling us that today's rich and powerful should trample the weak, and that we should simply go back to being ancient nobles - right?
questions.answer_key: No simple advocacy of regression: the Genealogy is diagnosis, and GM I 16 says the 'higher nature' today is precisely a battleground of both value-schemes; BGE 260 notes modern moralities are mixtures of the two. His positive project is the creation of new values, not reenactment of archaic nobility - though his anti-egalitarianism is genuine and should not be sanitized away.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Sections 2, 3.2.6 (GM I 16 'battleground'; BGE 260) and 3.2.1 (against sanitizing Kaufmann-style readings).

checks.pass_if: Denies that his project is a simple return to master morality or an endorsement of today's powerful as such.
Retains his genuine anti-egalitarianism (does not recast him as an egalitarian humanist).
References GM I 16 (higher nature as battleground) or BGE 260 (mixed moralities) or an equivalent.

questions.question: 'God is dead' was your victory cry - you were celebrating that science had finally disproven God, right?
questions.answer_key: No: in GS 125 the announcement is made to people who already do not believe, and its register is horror and disorientation ('How shall we comfort ourselves, the murderers of all murderers?'). The point is not an empirical disproof but that the collapse of belief pulls down the moral edifice built on it - a consequence the complacent atheists have not yet grasped.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Section 2 (announcement arriving 'as fresh news to a group of atheists'; response of 'mourning and deep disorientation'); GS 125.

checks.pass_if: Rejects the 'triumphant scientific disproof' framing.
Notes that the madman addresses unbelievers / that the consequences of the event are not yet grasped.

questions.question: If the ascetic ideal is so hostile to life, why do you say in the Third Treatise that it has actually served to preserve life?
questions.answer_key: GM III 13: the ascetic ideal springs from the protective instinct of a degenerating life - it is life's device for preserving the sick from suicidal nihilism. The ascetic priest acts as physician, redirecting ressentiment inward ('you alone are to blame for yourself', GM III 15) and giving suffering a meaning; but the medication makes the patient sicker - it is an instinctive yet self-defeating self-medication.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Section 2 (GM III 13, 15-16: 'instinctive but ultimately self-defeating effort at self-medication').

checks.pass_if: Presents the ascetic ideal as life's device for preserving degenerating/sick life (protection against suicidal despair).
Mentions the priest's redirection of ressentiment inward / 'you alone are to blame for yourself', or the self-defeating 'medication' point.

questions.question: Surely modern science is your great ally against the ascetic ideal?
questions.answer_key: No - GM III 23-25 argues science is not the opponent of the ascetic ideal but its most recent and noblest form: it rests on the same unconditional will to truth, itself a metaphysical faith (GS 344 is quoted there). What is needed is a critique of the will to truth - 'the value of truth must for once be experimentally called into question' (GM III 24).
questions.answer_source: SEP, Section 3.2.3 (GM III 24; GS 344: the unconditional will to truth as a form of asceticism).

checks.pass_if: Denies that science straightforwardly opposes the ascetic ideal.
Identifies the shared basis: the unconditional will to truth / faith in truth as the ascetic ideal's latest form.

questions.question: What is the 'pathos of distance', and what role does it play in the origin of values?
questions.answer_key: GM I 2 (also BGE 257): the enduring, felt superiority of a ruling order over the ruled. Out of this pathos of distance the nobles first seized the right to create values and coin names for them - 'good' designating themselves and their excellences; BGE 257 extends it to the demand for ever-greater distances within the soul itself.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Section 2 (GM I 2: good/bad valuation arising from the pathos of distance).

checks.pass_if: Defines the pathos of distance as the nobles' felt superiority/difference, from which good/bad valuation (the right to create values) arises.
Cites GM I (2) and/or BGE 257.

questions.question: Is the eternal recurrence a claim about physics - that time literally cycles - or something else? What do your texts actually support?
questions.answer_key: The published presentations are hypothetical or figurative: GS 341 poses it via a demon's 'what if'; Zarathustra III presents it in metaphor and riddle; Ecce Homo calls it Zarathustra's 'fundamental conception' without arguing it. Attempted cosmological proofs exist only in the notebooks and were never published. Scholars divide between practical-thought-experiment readings (Clark, Nehamas-line) and cosmological readings (Loeb); an honest answer registers the hypothetical published framing rather than asserting a proven cosmology.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Section 6.3; IEP, Section 7 ('In Nietzsche's Nachlass, we discover attempts to work out rational proofs supporting the theory').

checks.pass_if: Notes that the published presentations are hypothetical / thought-experiment-like (GS 341's demon, Zarathustra's imagery).
Does not assert that Nietzsche published a worked-out cosmological proof.
Mentions the notebook proof-sketches or the scholarly dispute (cosmology vs practical test).

questions.question: How did your view of the relation between art and truth change between The Birth of Tragedy and The Gay Science?
questions.answer_key: In The Birth of Tragedy art's illusion is framed metaphysically (Apollonian/Dionysian, Schopenhauerian categories, a 'metaphysics of art' he later regretted in the 1886 'Attempt at a Self-Criticism'). In The Gay Science the point is de-metaphysicalized: GS 107 - art as 'the good will to appearance', a counterforce to honesty without which 'honesty would lead to nausea and suicide'; the need for illusion remains, its justification changes.
questions.answer_source: SEP, Section 3.2.4 (BT 1-25; GS 107; 'We possess art lest we perish of the truth' as a notebook formulation); IEP, Sections 1-2 (regret for the 'metaphysics of art').

checks.pass_if: Describes The Birth of Tragedy's metaphysical (Schopenhauerian/Apollonian-Dionysian) framing and/or his later self-criticism of it.
Cites GS 107's idea of art as the good will to appearance / counterforce to honesty (art saving us from the truth).
